Script:


POPPIE NONGENA V/O: The long-awaited film Poppie Nongena, recently premiered at Kyknet’s Silwerskermfees in Camps Bay, It won 11 awards, including Best Feature Film. Official: Poppie! Poppie: Ja, meneer.

V/O: Adapted from Elsa Joubert’s book Die Swerfjare van Poppie Nongena, it tells the story of a domestic worker’s struggle with the pass laws, and the cruel effects of apartheid on black families. Official: Jy moet gaan.

V/O: Poppie Nongena was based on the life story of Elsa Joubert’s domestic worker Eunice. Even though she was born in Upington and lived in Cape Town, Eunice and her children were forced to move to the Ciskei. Sfx: Look, Bophuthatswana for the Tswana; For the Pedis it’s Lebowa. Kwazulu for the Zulus, and for the Xhosa it’s the Transkei and Ciskei. Because the Transkei has been declared independent, you’re no longer considered a South African citizen. I don’t understand. You’re an immigrant in your own land.
Max: I would say it’s probably one of the most important books ever written in Afrikaans.

V/O: Author and columnist, Max du Preez, is the founding editor of the Vrye Weekblad.

Max: The Poppie Nongena book was so powerful partly because of Elsa Joubert’s popularity as a mainstream, establishment writer, but also because it wasn't a political book. She wasn't in the struggle. She didn't protest against anything. There was no ideology in this book. It was the story of one human being. And it was so authentic, also because it was based on the truth, that it rang true. It was deeply moving to people and it was in Afrikaans.

V/O: Professor Sylvia Vollenhoven is an author and filmmaker who chairs the Alan Paton Literary Award jury. Sylvia: I remember reading the book and thinking wow! This is something else. This is so unusual, not just for a White writer, but for a White Afrikaans writer it was exceptional. Max: For the first time for the overwhelming majority of Afrikaans readers they could follow the story of a human being who suffered and was traumatized greatly by them.

V/O: As a journalist who had been covering those stories about the pass laws and concerned about apartheid, had been very close to the student movement and the uprisings of the 70’s, this was the first time I’d experienced a White writer delving into the issues that mattered for me, in a way that made sense to me.

Max: A very powerful cabinet minister's wife read this book in the local book club and she went home to her husband - the cabinet minister - and she was sort of red faced and flustered and she smacked the book down and she said “Good Lord, Papa! Is this what you’re doing to people?
Sfx: Protest

V/O: Although it touches on the student uprisings, the story highlights the systemic brutality of apartheid. Nico: This resembled or illustrated structural violence. Everyone thought about violence, just what happens in the street, in riots in police shooting, in attacks. But the book illustrated the system as structural violence, this absolutely breaking up of families, of moving people, no sense of humanity and that also gave a new light to the book. Poppie then being a symbol of a system that denied people their dignity.

V/O: The book received multiple awards and was translated into 13 languages. The play toured the world to packed houses, but this is the first feature film ever made. Elsa Joubert is now 96 years-old and lives in this retirement home in Cape Town, but was too frail for an interview. Her son, Nico Steytler, recalls that time. Claire: What memories do you have of the real Poppie, Eunice Ntsatha? Nico: The memory I have is this very warm person, a real personality that just embraced you. I remember coming back from a holiday, unexpected at home and she opened the door and she just said, “My God, boetie!” Well, this is coming in exactly that December that the movie takes place. Link: This is the house where Elsa Joubert formed a close relationship with her domestic worker, Poppie Nongena. Poppie’s real name was Notombizodumo Eunice Ntsatha, and she received royalties from the book until her dying day in 1992.

V/O: The movie was filmed in Oranjezicht, in the same road where Elsa Joubert lived. The character of Poppie, is played by Clementine Mosimane. Clementine: In every household there’s a Poppie. In South Africa there’s a Poppie Nongena in their own respective ways. So because of the ladies, the women, the mothers who are telling us their stories as kitchen girls, I drew from that. My granny herself was a kitchen girl. So their stories came to mind, and then I had to wear those caps, and just make them one cap and bring them together.

Sfx: Gee my jou pas. Ek sal gou-gou hoor of hulle jou op my naam sal registreer. JUlle twee moet net hier sit. Chrissi hoor jy my? Ja mama. Jy klim nie uit nie. Ja mevrou. V/O: The role of the madam, Mrs Swanepoel, is played by Anna-Mart van der Merwe. Anna-Mart: You have two women that in the right circumstance would have been incredible friends. But because of the racial divide, because of the time they were in, there was this immense sadness for me because two women looking at each other and they know they like soulmates but it's like looking they had a window between them the whole time. And I for me that was quite profound and wonderful. Sorry, I just want to. But yeah. And that's Elsa's genius but it's also Clementine’s genius.

Sfx: Ek verstaan hoe jy voel, maar jy moet aanhou! Hoe kan jy se jy verstaan? Jy weet nie wat dit is om ‘n swart vrou in hierdie land te wees nie. Poppie, ek het prober, ek sweer. Ek sweer ek het prober. Kom hierso mevrou. Ek weet jy het. Maar vee asseblief daai trane af. Hulle kan my nie help nie. V/O: The director and co-screenwriter is rising star, Christiaan Olwagen.

Christiaan: The script was the bones and Clementine came in and she gave it that beating heart, and really fleshed it out into a complete human being. She became Poppie. Link: The book was published over 40 years ago, and so much has since changed, one can’t help but wonder whether the story is still relevant for this generation of South Africans.

Sylvia: That particular story might have lost a bit of its currency in a modern sense, but the issue remains and the issue is no longer so much an issue of race, it's just an issue of class and how South Africans take domestic workers for granted and how little rights these women have cloistered in homes and without too much connection with each other.

Clementine: For me it’s still relevant. For me the woman is still fighting a battle. Women are fighting for so many thing to be on the right level with men. It’s in the workplace. It’s in the home, it’s in society.

Sfx: Ek wil toilet toe. Hoekom het jy nie by die huis gegaan nie? Mama was te haastig. Ai Chrissie, kan jy knyp? Nee.

V/O: Christiaan is sensitive to the role of domestic workers in caring for their employer’s children. He, himself, was raised by a caretaker. Christiaan: Her name was Anna. Anna Mchenge. And when I read this book I saw her on every page and every glance, every scold, every prayer And selfishly I decided that this was going to be my love letter to her.

Claire: Are you going to show it to her, and what will you say before she sees it? Christiaan: I think she’ll understand the intention and I think she will understand that I’m saying thank you for being such a massive contribution to my life. And although you were paid to look after me, you weren’t paid to love me – but you did that anyway
